speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: My response will address related oral and written questions on wealth inequality and wealth data filed by Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Gerald Giam1,2,3 and Mr Louis Chua scheduled for subsequent Sittings.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: If Members are satisfied with the response, they may wish to withdraw their questions after this session.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: These outcomes reflect sustained policies to uplift lower-income workers and foster inclusive growth, supported by a progressive system of taxes and transfers.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Most countries face challenges in measuring wealth inequality accurately.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Certain assets such as unlisted businesses, private equity and overseas assets, are inherently difficult to track and value.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have made our best effort by combining survey data from the Household Expenditure Survey with administrative records.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The survey captures information on assets such as bank deposits and unlisted assets, including overseas assets, and liabilities such as household arrears and bank loans.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We augment this with administrative data on properties, Central Provident Fund (CPF) accounts, Singapore Savings Bonds, shares and securities held in Central Depository accounts and the CPF Investment Scheme Special Account, life insurance policies, balances in the Post-Secondary Education Account and Edusave accounts, and Housing and Development Board (HDB)-administered loans.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Property values are estimated based on their fair market value.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have progressively improved the coverage and quality of wealth data captured in the Household Expenditure Survey.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We will continue to study how data collection methods can be strengthened.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This is our first compilation of the wealth Gini coefficient and we do not have a historical series.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We intend to track this measure over time.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And we will consider whether additional indicators, which Members have suggested, can be provided.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Members asked for further breakdowns of wealth inequality – such as by asset type, housing type or age cohort.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Gini coefficient is measured at the household and not individual level.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Hence, we do not break it down by age cohorts.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We do not compute Gini coefficients by asset type, as households can and do convert their wealth from one asset type to another.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We also do not differentiate between public and private housing, or between owner-occupied and non-owner-occupied housing, in computing the wealth Gini, as this a stock measure of net worth and not a measure of liquidity.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We do not have sufficiently granular data at the moment to provide the breakdown between local and overseas holdings.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about wealth concentration at the top.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: These levels are broadly comparable to advanced economies with similar wealth Gini coefficients.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: However, these estimates should be interpreted with caution, due to sample size limitations and potential under-reporting in survey responses at both ends of the distribution.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Wealth inequality is higher than income inequality in all advanced economies, as wealth accumulates over the life-cycle.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In Singapore, a significant part of household wealth, especially among lower- and middle-income households, is held in owner-occupied housing and CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Our housing and CPF policies have enabled many Singaporeans to build their assets over time.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This broad-based asset ownership helps to moderate inequality while strengthening long-term security and social stability.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Mr Yip and Mr Giam asked whether we have considered other forms of wealth taxes beyond property tax.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This is why we focus on less mobile assets like property and motor vehicles.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: These taxes are progressive, with higher-value assets taxed at higher rates.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Younger households who are still accumulating assets should not be unduly burdened.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: At the same time, higher-value property owners should contribute more.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: For asset-rich but income-poor seniors, we provide deferral mechanisms for property tax payments to ease cash-flow pressures.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We fully agree with Ms Mariam Jaafar on the need to sustain upward social mobility for current and future cohorts.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Our strategy is to intervene early, provide support through life and ensure wage progression.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have expanded access to affordable and quality preschool education to give children from all backgrounds a good start.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Our schools provide a strong foundation with more support for those from disadvantaged households.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: SkillsFuture provides continuing learning opportunities for adults, including enhanced support for mid-career workers.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Progressive Wage Model and Workfare raise earnings and strengthen career pathways for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: For families facing complex challenges, ComLink+ provides more intensive, coordinated support in partnership with community organisations.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Overall, Singapore remains in a stronger position than many advanced economies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But we do not take this for granted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The first is whether there are more proximal indicators of inequality?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I note that the Minister has said that the next survey will be conducted in 2028, but given the importance of wealth inequality and income inequality in our society, whether there are any attempts at capturing some of these more proximal indicators of inequality, both wealth and income?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: My second question relates back to the statistic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: How is the Ministry looking at using this statistic?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Are you looking at the trend or are you looking at the threshold and does that subsequently warrant the kinds of actions that you would take?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Wealth is notoriously hard to measure, particularly data on overseas assets and unlisted assets.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The current estimates, both wealth as well as income, are our best efforts, in line with best practices in other countries.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We will take into account some of the suggestions that are made by Members on what we can do.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In terms of household income trends, we already publish that data regularly, annually, in the Key Household Income Trends Report.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But for the wealth Gini coefficient and wealth data, it is dependent on the main source, which is the household expenditure survey, which we do every five years.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think the next cycle is in 2028.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And so, when that data is obtained, we will try our best to put out something regularly.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We intend to track this data, as I have explained.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The absolute numbers are an indication of where we are, relative to other countries, but the trending is also important, whether or not wealth Gini is going up or going down, in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The enhanced data and methodology that we have used for both income inequality as well as wealth inequality will improve our understanding of the states of inequality in Singapore, which will better help us develop more evidence-based and targeted policies to improve Singaporeans lives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is an issue very close to my heart.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, are there any early indicators for cohorts in the 1990s and the 2000s of the data on where they stand today in terms of upward mobility?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And does the Government have any targets; you talked about trends, but do you have targets for what you would like it to be at, in the next time we run this cycle?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And how are we evolving our policies for this?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And then, thirdly, as we think about artificial intelligence (AI) and technological shifts that are reshaping jobs, how are we ensuring that children from lower-income households are not disproportionately affected?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I think I raised this point in my Budget speech yesterday and I am very keen to hear what the Ministry is thinking about that.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The findings of the Occasional Paper indicate that the social outcomes in the past decade have been positive.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think it suggests that our strategy of combining inclusive economic growth with targeted and progressive support has had tangible impact.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But we do not take these outcomes for granted.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But we are encouraged that the increasing proportion of younger Singaporeans have attained higher levels of education and skills, and that will put them in good stead to be able to do well in life.
On her second question on the bottom quintile, the issues are more complex.

We are also working very hard to make sure that children in those households have a good start in life through preschool and that is part of the KidSTART programme, which we have initiated many years ago.
Sustaining social mobility will indeed be a challenge.
We will have to work extensively on families in the bottom quintile, knowing that the challenges to overcome are more complex and more difficult.

As for AI, the current crop of Singaporeans and the concerns about how they will need to adapt, I think the key is really through ensuring our Singaporeans are skilled, are able to adapt quickly, take on the new jobs that will be created in this new economy.
This will generate wage growth and hopefully then, in that way, they will be able to maintain a strong standard of living and continue to progress in life.
I think we have to work hard to lean against the structural pressures that will happen as our economy matures and develops, so that Singaporeans can succeed regardless of background.
We have to remain vigilant and to refine our policies when needed so that we can remain socially mobile over the long term.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The focus of my supplementary question is on seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For older Singaporeans who may own valuable property but have limited or no income, how does the Ministry assess the impact of the higher property taxes on the cost-of-living pressures?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note the Minister had earlier mentioned that there are current initiatives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But will there be additional safeguards to ensure that the measures aimed at reducing wealth inequality do not unintentionally strain retirees?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We recognise the concerns of the group that Mr Yip spoke about – the asset rich and cash poor retirees.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Investment properties and higher-value properties are taxed higher and homeowners with only one property are taxed lower and they receive property tax rebates when necessary.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope that more data on wealth inequality will be published as this could help us to craft policy solutions to reduce inequality in our country.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has the Ministry conducted a simulation on how much wealth Gini coefficient would be reduced if investment property equity were excluded, to isolate the impact of this type of equity on inequality?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand the Senior Minister of State's point just now that this can be tax planned away, but I would like to know the Government is trying and it sees this as a priority.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Because property value captures a broad range of different property characteristics, whether owner-occupied or not, as a store of value.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The wealth Gini coefficient is not a measure of liquidity.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It is a measure of the stock of wealth.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, that is the first point I would like to make.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Second is that for property, the way we have implemented it in Singapore is that we have taken a broad-based approach to ensure that Singaporeans have broad asset ownership, through HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And as a result, we should not necessarily compare what we do in Singapore, in terms of including housing, with other countries.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As I have explained, it is because we treat property as a store of wealth.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: There is no real need for us to do so and that is something at the moment that we will not do.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Today, we have an approach that works on the whole.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The outcomes of the past decade, in terms of our policies, have been positive.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have been able to achieve real income growth.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have been able to achieve a decline in inequality and we have been able to achieve a balance using both wealth taxation, as we explained, as well as income taxation.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As our society ages and we move towards an older society where there is more asset owning, that is something we can consider, whether or not we need a shift.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But we have to do this carefully so that we know that the outcomes that we want to achieve can be done so without too much social perturbation.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: What we do is that for household wealth, we do include both liquid and illiquid assets, because this is in line with international guidelines.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: All property owners, including those who own HDB flats, can rent out their property for income, and to sell it and keep the proceeds.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And so, it is up to how people manage it, how they activate this store of wealth that they can use.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And so, there is no real need for us, and it is not in international best practice for us to separate out investment versus non-investment properties or owner-occupied versus non-owner-occupied properties.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This is in line with international best practices and we will try to continue to do that, particularly since in Singapore, our approach is to encourage owner-occupation, and to encourage and make sure that Singapore has broad-based ownership, particularly through the ownership of their HDB flats.
